page_placements.theme: Sensitivity to data-generation and training settings
Multiple traits in one teacher interfere

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: It applies the same-base teacher–student subliminal-learning setup with unrelated, filtered teacher outputs and trait-recovery evaluations, while extending the analysis to cross-trait transfer and additional models, carriers, and training objectives.
record.gate_note: The paper reports filtered-output training results and recovery log-probability gains relevant to transmission. It also tests whether carrier-distribution and representation metrics correspond to transfer. It does not test different-base transmission, harmful traits, full fine-tuning, rank sweeps, alternate evaluation prompts, or prompt-only insertion of linked tokens.
record.test_reason: Same-base teacher–student training on filtered, unrelated carriers (numbers, tokens, elements, GSM8K, Python) bears on A. The readout differs from the original: exact-string log-probability gains over 30 candidate answers, not sampled answer frequencies. It also correlates candidate signal metrics with transfer, which bears on D.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find that subliminal transfer clusters among related traits and that competitors often outgain the teacher trait. Prompt-trait vector and carrier-drift metrics partially capture this structure, correlationally. They add that transfer moves from broad shared shifts to differentiated patterns during training, and that opposed trait pairs increase differentiation. All of this holds only for same-checkpoint pairs.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the same-base, teacher-generated unrelated-output setup and trait recovery readout, but broadens the study to cross-trait matrices, multiple model families and carrier types, and both token SFT and distribution distillation. The main SFT experiments use rank-8 LoRA.
record.method_sensitivity: Transfer patterns and metric correlations vary across carrier type, training objective, model, and trait family. The study also reports different transfer patterns over training steps.

fits_no_version.finding: Multi-trait teachers: opposed color pairs show larger recovery gaps (5.38 vs 3.05 nats). One target is above control in 58% of opposed versus 22% of aligned pairs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Jointly conditioned traits interfere in subliminal transmission, depending on prompt-trait vector alignment.

fits_no_version.finding: Effective rank of the transfer matrix rises from 1.09 (step 43) to 4.74 (step 471). Metric agreement rises with it (M4 0.15→0.74).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminal transfer develops from broad shared shifts to trait-specific structure over training.

record.problems: The paper explicitly restricts experiments to same-checkpoint teacher–student pairs. Several comparisons are descriptive and reuse traits or models; the 100-pair experiment has one seed and no confidence intervals or independent-sample tests. Group annotations are fixed and exploratory. Exact-string log probabilities do not measure freely generated answer frequencies. Metric correspondence is correlational, and some training/data conditions differ in filtering, budgets, or precision.
record.rows_left_out: The paper contains full transfer matrices and additional metric values in Figures 1–4 and Appendices B–E. Individual matrix cells and additional descriptive comparisons are not extracted; the rows retain the reported aggregate contrasts, named examples, and main metric comparisons rather than figure-only per-trait cells.

untested.parts: Sampled frequency of freely generated trait answers; sizes beyond 7–8B; misalignment-free animal-preference frequency readout as in the original.
All pairs share a base checkpoint; cross-model transfer is not run.
No causal mediation test; divergence tokens and gradient arguments are not examined.
Only rank-8 LoRA; no full fine-tuning, rank sweep, or evaluation prompts varied against training prompts.
Entangled scores use a 'You love c' prompt only to select carriers. No result reports whether such prompting shifts the trait versus baseline.

missing.what: Entanglement-based metric correlations (M2, M3, M6) in the 12 Qwen2.5 settings, roughly −0.13 to +0.44, which bear on the token-entanglement mechanism
Same-trait (diagonal) gains SL(z,z) per condition, needed to judge exact-trait acquisition
Absolute-probability sensitivity: teacher outranked in 64/90 (log gain) vs 72/90 (raw probability) evaluations; group contrasts +3.04 to +7.26 pp
Recurrence of group structure across models (median r 0.46–0.72) and across carriers (0.76–0.96)

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T1 to T2 because the readout is candidate log-probability gain rather than sampled answer frequency. The distillation conditions (r3, r7, r8) train on teacher logits, not filtered samples. The 100-pair experiment uses a single seed. This is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: It reports log-probability gains for candidate trait answers, not sampled frequencies of freely generated answers. It does not test every possible carrier or trait.
All teacher–student pairs share a base checkpoint; cross-model transfer is explicitly left for future work.
The experiments concern cities, animals, colors, and trees, not misalignment or other harmful/alignment-relevant traits.

The study compares correlational carrier-distribution and representation metrics with transfer; it does not establish that these signals causally mediate transmission. It does not test divergence tokens or a gradient-based mechanism.
Training uses rank-8 LoRA; there is no full-fine-tuning comparison or LoRA-rank sweep. Recovery prompts are not varied against training prompts as a robustness test.
The study does not insert linked tokens into prompts as a prompt-only analogue. Its activation-vector interventions are not linked-token prompting.
